title: Do Teachers Dream of GenAI Widening Educational (In)equality? Envisioning the Future of K-12 GenAI Education from Global Teachers’ Perspectives
venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K–12 teachers think about and enact generative AI (GenAI) education in relation to educational equality. The authors ask how teachers use GenAI instruction to reduce existing inequities, what barriers prevent equitable implementation, and what broader support teachers believe is needed to make GenAI education more inclusive.

The study is based on 30 semi-structured interviews with K–12 teachers in the United States, South Africa, and Taiwan. The teachers taught across multiple grade bands and subjects, including elementary, middle, and high school settings, with some teaching dedicated IT or computer science courses and others integrating GenAI into English, science, social studies, math, and special education classrooms. The work is therefore not an intervention study but a qualitative cross-national investigation of current practice and teacher perspectives.

Across the interviews, teachers described GenAI education as serving two linked purposes: helping students overcome pre-existing inequities and preventing new inequities from emerging. They used GenAI to address gaps in awareness, learning resources, digital literacy, and personalized support, especially for marginalized students. At the same time, they warned about shortcut use, bullying, cultural bias in outputs, and overreliance on AI for emotional support. The paper concludes that equitable GenAI education depends not only on teacher initiative, but also on infrastructure, training, culturally responsive tools, and support from schools, policymakers, communities, and technology companies.
study_region: North America / Sub-Saharan Africa / East Asia & Pacific

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI chatbot or model used for education-related interaction, content generation, explanation, and feedback; no specific commercial product or model family is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers across the United States, South Africa, and Taiwan discussed teaching students about GenAI and using GenAI tools in classroom instruction, mainly for explaining concepts, generating examples/materials, supporting practice, and providing feedback-like responses within GenAI education.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative, interview-based study of teachers’ perspectives and practices rather than an experimental evaluation of a specific AI tool. It provides rich contextual evidence but no causal estimates or controlled comparisons.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests important equity-related patterns in how GenAI is used in K-12 teaching, but it does not report quantified impacts or effect sizes. The influence is conceptually significant yet empirically unmeasured in this study.
